```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_bsvarSIGNs <- requireNamespace("bsvarSIGNs", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE,
    comment  = "#>",
    fig.width  = 7,
    fig.height = 5,
    dpi = 100,
    eval = has_bsvarSIGNs
)
options(mcmc.pb = FALSE)
```

```{r}
library(acpbvar)
```

This second vignette uses the standard sign-restriction example in
structural VARs, following Uhlig (2005). It is the reference exercise for
studying the effects of monetary policy shocks on U.S. output, identified by
signs only, and it imposes the signs on several horizons. The data are
available through the R package bsvarSIGNs, which must be installed: if it
is missing, the code chunks below are not run.

## 1. The data

The `monetary` dataset of bsvarSIGNs is sourced from the replication
package of Antolín-Díaz and Rubio-Ramírez (2018). It comprises six monthly
time series spanning January 1965 to August 2007 (Uhlig stops in 2003):
real GDP, GDP deflator, consumer price index (CPI), total reserves and
non-borrowed reserves, all in logarithms, and the federal funds rate in
percentage points. The logarithmic values are multiplied by 100 here, so
that the responses read as percentages.

```{r}
data("monetary", package = "bsvarSIGNs")
Y <- as.matrix(monetary)
Y[, 1:5] <- 100 * Y[, 1:5]
var_names <- c("real GDP", "GDP deflator", "CPI", "total reserves",
               "non-borrowed reserves", "fed funds")
colnames(Y) <- var_names
dim(Y)
round(head(Y, 3), 2)
```

## 2. The model

The model under consideration is a VAR(12), consistent with the approach in
Uhlig (2005). The hyperparameters $\kappa_1$ and $\kappa_2$ are selected by
Empirical Bayes. The total number of draws is fixed at 1000; the chunk prints
the selected hyperparameters, the convergence code and the elapsed time.

```{r}
p <- 12L
t_post <- system.time(
    mcmc <- post_sim(Y, p = p, R = 1000L, var_names = var_names, seed = 1)
)
round(mcmc$spec$kappa, 4)
mcmc$spec$convergence
t_post[["elapsed"]]
```

## 3. The identification of Uhlig (2005)

A single shock is identified (`n_id = 1`, `S` is a row vector). According
to Uhlig, after a contractionary monetary policy shock prices (deflator,
CPI) and non-borrowed reserves do not rise, as the Federal Reserve drains
liquidity, and the federal funds rate does not fall. The entry for real GDP
is zero, i.e. unrestricted: the effect on output is the question of the
exercise and is not imposed. Total reserves are also left unrestricted,
since their sign is not determined a priori. The horizon is set to 5, as
Uhlig imposes the sign restrictions on impact and for the following five
months; thus h ranges from 0 to 5. The chunk returns the row vector `S`,
the indices of the discarded draws (none here) and the summary of the
number of rotations tried per draw.

```{r}
S <- matrix(c(0, -1, -1, 0, -1, 1), nrow = 1,
            dimnames = list("monetary", var_names))
S
t_sign <- system.time(
    accepted <- sign_restrict(mcmc, S, horizons = 5L, max_tries = 20000L, verbose = FALSE)
)
length(accepted)
attr(accepted, "failed_draws")
summary(attr(accepted, "n_tries"))
t_sign[["elapsed"]]
```

## 4. The responses

The maximum impulse response horizon is set to 24 months. The impulse
response functions (IRFs) include six shocks, although only the first shock
is identified, so only its slice is kept. `plot_irfs()` draws the response
of each variable to the monetary policy shock, with the posterior median
and the 16-84 band.

```{r, fig.height = 9}
H <- 24L
irfs <- collect_irfs(accepted, n = 6L, p = p, H = H)
irf_mp <- irfs[, , 1, , drop = FALSE]          # the identified shock only
plot_irfs(irf_mp, var_names = var_names, shock_names = "monetary policy",
          probs = c(0.16, 0.84))
```

The second chunk provides the output trajectory, including the median and
the 16th to 84th percentile equal-tailed credible band at h ∈ {0, 6, 12, 24}
months. The findings of Uhlig are corroborated: there is no clear evidence
that a monetary tightening reduces real GDP, as the credible bands encompass
zero at every horizon and the median is even positive in the first months.

```{r}
path <- apply(irf_mp[1, , 1, ], 1, stats::quantile, probs = c(0.16, 0.5, 0.84))
colnames(path) <- paste0("h", 0:H)
round(path[, c(1, 7, 13, 25)], 3)             # real GDP after a monetary tightening
```

## 5. Comparison with bsvarSIGNs

This section replicates the same procedure using bsvarSIGNs (Wang and
Woźniak), which is characterised by the Minnesota prior of Giannone, Lenza
and Primiceri with sum-of-coefficients and single-unit-root dummy
observations. In bsvarSIGNs the hyperparameters can be estimated by a
separate adaptive Metropolis step (`estimate_hyper()`), which is not called
here: they are kept at the package defaults. The sampler is implemented in
C++. The `sign_irf` argument of bsvarSIGNs is a
three-dimensional array structured as variable by shock by horizon, where
`NA` indicates an unrestricted response. In acpbvar, the matrix `S` is
structured as shock by variable, with 0 indicating an unrestricted response.
The number of draws remains the same, and only a single core is used.

```{r}
sign_irf <- matrix(NA, 6, 6)
sign_irf[, 1] <- c(NA, -1, -1, NA, -1, 1)      # variable x shock, horizon 0
sign_irf <- array(sign_irf, dim = c(6, 6, 6))  # horizons 0..5
set.seed(1)
t_bs <- system.time({
    spec_bs <- bsvarSIGNs::specify_bsvarSIGN$new(Y, p = p, sign_irf = sign_irf, mc.cores = 1)
    post_bs <- bsvars::estimate(spec_bs, S = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
    irf_bs  <- bsvars::compute_impulse_responses(post_bs, horizon = H)
})
dim(irf_bs)                                   # variable x shock x horizon x draw
t_bs[["elapsed"]]
```

The plot presents the median responses to the monetary shock, displaying
acpbvar in black and bsvarSIGNs in red. For values of h between 0 and 5,
where the signs bind, and in the following months the two medians overlap
on all six series; they diverge at longer horizons on real GDP and reserves,
where the data are weak and the influence of the prior distributions
increases: the dummy observations of the Minnesota prior, at the default
hyperparameters, sustain the persistence of the responses, while the
asymmetric conjugate prior lets them decay. The
differences lie within the credible bands of either package. The table below
reports the elapsed seconds on the machine that rendered the vignette.

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
med_ac <- apply(irf_mp[, , 1, ], c(1, 2), stats::median)
med_bs <- apply(irf_bs[, 1, , ], c(1, 2), stats::median)
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(2.5, 2.5, 2, 0.5), mgp = c(1.4, 0.4, 0))
for (j in 1:6) {
    ylim <- range(med_ac[j, ], med_bs[j, ])
    plot(0:H, med_ac[j, ], type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = ylim, xlab = "", ylab = "",
         main = var_names[j], cex.main = 0.9)
    lines(0:H, med_bs[j, ], lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
    abline(h = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
    if (j == 1) legend("topright", c("acpbvar", "bsvarSIGNs"), lwd = 2,
                       lty = c(1, 2), col = c("black", "firebrick"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}
par(op)
```

```{r}
data.frame(package = c("acpbvar", "bsvarSIGNs"),
           seconds = round(c(t_post[["elapsed"]] + t_sign[["elapsed"]], t_bs[["elapsed"]]), 1))
```

## 6. The joint acceptance method

The identification is repeated using `method = "joint"`, where each draw
is associated with a single rotation, and the draws whose rotation does not
satisfy the signs are discarded. Since the per-draw search needed 16
rotations on average, about one draw in sixteen survives. Achieving the
same precision as the `per_draw` method requires setting `R` to several
tens of thousands.

```{r}
accepted_joint <- sign_restrict(mcmc, S, horizons = 5L, method = "joint", verbose = FALSE)
length(accepted_joint)
```

## References

- Antolín-Díaz, J., & Rubio-Ramírez, J. F. (2018). Narrative Sign
  Restrictions for SVARs. *American Economic Review*, 108(10), 2802-2829.
- Chan, J. C. C. (2022). Asymmetric conjugate priors for large Bayesian
  VARs. *Quantitative Economics*, 13(3), 1145-1169.
- Giannone, D., Lenza, M., & Primiceri, G. E. (2015). Prior Selection for
  Vector Autoregressions. *Review of Economics and Statistics*, 97(2),
  436-451.
- Uhlig, H. (2005). What are the effects of monetary policy on output?
  Results from an agnostic identification procedure. *Journal of Monetary
  Economics*, 52(2), 381-419.
- Wang, X., & Woźniak, T. (2025). bsvarSIGNs: Bayesian SVARs with Sign,
  Zero, and Narrative Restrictions. R package version 3.0,
  <https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.bsvarSIGNs>.
